newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. moves to clean up Rwanda tribunal structures.
newsitem.headline: U.N. moves to clean up Rwanda tribunal structures.

text.p: As the Rwanda war crimes tribunal delayed its proceedings on Thursday, the United Nations said it was sending new personnel to correct the alleged mismangement of the court.

Secretary-General Kofi Annan said through his spokesman he would take "decisive action" to make changes in the administrative apparatus of the tribunal, plagued by problems since its inception in the Tanzanian town of Arusha.

"The moral weight of this body is enormous and those responsible for carrying out that work must meet the highest ethical and professional standards," he said, according to U.N. spokesman Fred Eckhard.
Karl Paschke of Germany, the U.N. inspector general, has prepared a report on the alleged abuses in the tribunal, and Eckhard said Annan would take action once he had a chance to review it.
"But even before it is complete changes have and will be made in the administrative areas of the tribunal."

The tribunal was set up by the U.N. Security Council to prosecute genocide in Rwanda in 1994. After a brief start it adjourned on Thursday when the prosecution failed to present witnesses because they had not arrived from Rwanda. It plans to continue on Friday.

Rwanda swiftly blamed the tribunal for the snag, saying it applied for travel documents for the witnesses only two days ago. Tribunal officials said 31 witnesses due to testify against Hutu former government official Jean-Paul Akayesu had encountered visa problems.
Akayesu, 43, is charged with genocide and crimes against humanity during the four-month slaughter that resulted in more than 500,000 deaths of Tutsis and moderate Hutus.
Eckhard said a new acting chief of administration, Mohammed Said of Ethiopia, had been sent to Arusha last month, replacing George Anderson of Liberia who had left in October.

In addition, Mario Cianci, who holds Italian and U.S. nationality, was going to Arusha soon to temporarily take over personnel. That position is held by Andronico Adede of Kenya, a legal officer who worked in New York for U.N. Undersecretary-General Hans Corell of Sweden.

The Arusha controversy is fraught with racial overtones, with European employees complaining that the tribunal's administrators have given jobs to relatives and friends who have no qualifications and discriminated against non-Africans.
U.N. officials said they believed Africans would be replacing those expected to be released from their jobs.
They admitted privately that the problems were the result of a misperception of New York's responsibilities in the tribunal, which was to function as an independent entity.
But in the last few months officials have realised that judicial independence did not mean neglecting administrative structures.

Arusha was an unlikely venue for the tribunal, with primitive telephone and other communication links. The tribunal has indicted 21 people, seven of whom are held in Aurusha. Another eight are still at large and four are in detention in Cameroon. The United States and Switzerland hold one each.

Among four held in Cameroon is Colonel Theoneste Bagosora, described as giving military orders at the beginning of the 1994 massacres. His transfer has been delayed but tribunal officials said on Thursday an agreement had been signed with Cameroon for the transfer.
